subtitle: The October 1989 status report on which Internet protocols were at which stage of standardization.

tldr.problem: The Internet needed a clear, authoritative list of which protocols were official standards, which were being considered, and which were experimental or obsolete.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC documents the Internet standardization process and lists all protocols in each standardization state (standard, draft standard, proposed, experimental, historic) and status (required, recommended, elective, not recommended).
tldr.outcome: It served as the official reference for Internet protocol standardization in late 1989 and was itself updated periodically as new protocols advanced through the standards track.

facts.label: Standardization states
facts.value: 5: Standard, Draft Standard, Proposed, Experimental, Historic

today: RFC 1140 replaced this document. RFC 1130 is historic and serves as a snapshot of Internet protocol standardization as it stood in October 1989.

sections.title: The IAB and Protocol Standardization
sections.content:
RFC 1130 is the October 1989 status report from the Internet Activities Board describing which protocols are official Internet standards and at what stage each protocol stands. The IAB maintains this list to coordinate the evolution of Internet protocols as they become increasingly used in commercial settings.

The document explains that the IAB receives protocol proposals from the Internet community, assigns them to task forces or working groups for review and development, and passes them through an IESG (Internet Engineering Steering Group) review. The general policy is that protocols gain implementation experience before receiving official standard status. The IAB reserves the use of the term "standard" in any RFC to only those protocols it has explicitly approved.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet board keeps track of which network rules are official, which are being tested, and which are old or not recommended. This document is their status report for fall 1989.

sections.title: The Standardization Process
sections.content:
The RFC explains how protocols move through standardization stages. Anyone can invent, document, implement, and test a protocol; the IAB encourages documenting all protocols in the RFC series even if they never become standards. Experimental protocols are those developed as part of research projects, not intended for operational use. Proposed protocols may become standards in the future and should be implemented and tested by several groups. Draft Standard protocols are actively being considered by the IAB and require substantial testing and community comment. Standard protocols are official Internet standards declared by the IAB.

Historic protocols have been superseded or abandoned and are at an evolutionary dead end. In addition to standardization state, protocols receive a separate status designation: Required (all systems must implement), Recommended (all systems should implement), Elective (systems may implement), or Not Recommended (limited, specialized, or problematic protocols).
sections.plainLanguage: Protocols start as ideas that people test. If they work well, they become proposed, then draft, then standard. Some get dropped because they don't work well or get replaced by better ones.

sections.title: RFC Documents and Related Reference Materials
sections.content:
The RFC document series serves as the primary publication venue for all Internet protocol specifications and testing results. Once an RFC is issued, it is never revised or reissued with the same number, though a protocol may be documented in multiple different RFCs as it evolves. The document emphasizes the importance of checking this "IAB Official Protocol Standards" memo to determine which RFC contains the current specification of each protocol.

Related reference documents that work alongside this standards list include the "Assigned Numbers" (RFC 1010), which lists assigned values for protocol fields like IP protocol codes and TCP port numbers; the "Official Protocols" (RFC 1011), which describes known problems and experiments with each protocol; the "Gateway Requirements" (RFC 1009); and the "Host Requirements" (RFC 1122 and RFC 1123). The document notes that the Internet community specifications for IP and TCP (RFC 791, RFC 793) align with DoD MIL-STD specifications and should be used together.
sections.plainLanguage: All the official rulebooks are published in a series called RFCs. This document points you to which RFC has the latest version of each rule.

sections.title: Explanation of Standardization States and Status
sections.content:
A protocol's standardization state is one of: Standard (established as official), Draft Standard (under active consideration), Proposed (may be considered for standardization), Experimental (for research use), or Historic (superseded or abandoned). These represent how far along the protocol is in the standards process.

A protocol's status independently indicates how broadly it should be implemented: Required protocols must be in all systems, Recommended protocols should be in all systems, Elective protocols may be implemented when needed, and Not Recommended protocols have limited or problematic applicability. Most systems will be on the main diagonal of the state/status matrix, with new protocols starting as Proposed/Elective or Experimental/Not Recommended, and mature protocols at Standard/Required or Standard/Recommended.

The document notes that few protocols are required in all systems because Internet hosts are diverse (gateways, terminal servers, workstations, general-purpose hosts). However, general-purpose hosts are expected to implement at least IP (with ICMP), TCP, UDP, Telnet, FTP, SMTP, Mail, and the Domain Name System.
sections.plainLanguage: Each protocol has two tags: where it is in the approval process (experimental, proposed, draft, or standard), and how important it is (required, recommended, optional, or not recommended).

sections.title: The Protocol Lists
sections.content:
The document lists protocols organized by their standardization state. Standard Protocols include the foundational suite: IP, ICMP, TCP, UDP, SMTP, Telnet, and FTP. It also lists Specific Standard Protocols for transmitting IP over various physical networks (Ethernet, X.25, ARCNET, FDDI, etc.). Draft Standard Protocols include TFTP, SNMP, and the Mail Privacy procedures (RFCs 1113-1115). Proposed Protocols range from NFS and NNTP to Finger and SUPDUP. Experimental Protocols include BGP, IP multicast routing, and TCP extensions. Historic Protocols are protocols that have been superseded, such as GGP, HMP, and the old Host Monitoring Protocol, marked as not recommended.

Notable recent additions listed in the "Recent Changes" section include Host Requirements (now required standard), Network Time Protocol (now recommended), Internet Group Multicast Protocol (now recommended), and the Mail Privacy procedures advancing to draft standard status.
sections.plainLanguage: The document lists which protocols are in each category: some are finished and official, some are still being tested, some are old and shouldn't be used anymore.
